title: Apple: Ancient Apple Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: Two grafts of Newton's Woolsthorpe apple, at Trinity College and MIT, plus an Arizona orchard planted in 1912 and still flowering every spring.
intro: Two of the apple trees on this map descend from the one Isaac Newton knew at Woolsthorpe Manor, which died around 1815 to 1820. An apple variety travels only by grafting, so each is the old tree carried on in new wood. Trinity College in Cambridge planted its graft in 1954 below the room Newton had as a student. MIT's stands in the President's Garden off the Infinite Corridor, and in 2009 a Tufts grounds manager drove over and cut three branches from it. Both are 'Flower of Kent', a coarse cooking apple nobody grows for flavour. The other two are working trees. Frank Pendley began his orchard in Oak Creek Canyon, Arizona, in 1912, and its nearly 300 trees still flower each spring in Slide Rock State Park. In Milton Keynes, a row of old, hollowed trunks along a path in Linford Wood all lean the same way.
